prompt.context_jp: 昼前から客が入り始めた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 坂本さん＿暖簾をくぐったのは十一時過ぎだった。
prompt.prompt_en: Sakamoto-san is being introduced into the scene as a new arrival. Which particle fits?

feedback.correct_en: Sakamoto-san enters the narrative here as new information — the focus is on the event of someone arriving — so が marks him as the freshly introduced subject of 'the one who came through the noren.'
feedback.incorrect_en: は would treat Sakamoto-san as an already-established topic the sentence comments on, but he hasn't been mentioned yet; that makes him sound oddly pre-known.

contrast_examples.en: Sakamoto-san came. (announcing his arrival)
Sakamoto-san is a regular. (commenting on the known person)

prompt.prompt_jp: と美香は笑ったが、目＿笑っていなかった。
prompt.prompt_en: Mika laughed, but the line draws a contrast with her eyes. Which particle fits the blank?

feedback.correct_en: は here is contrastive: she laughed, but as for her eyes specifically, they were not. Marking 目 with は sets the eyes against the laughing mouth.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would simply report 'her eyes weren't laughing' as new information, losing the deliberate 'mouth yes / eyes no' contrast that makes the line work.

contrast_examples.jp: 口は笑っていたが、目は笑っていなかった。
contrast_examples.en: Her mouth was smiling, but her eyes weren't. (contrast)

contrast_examples.jp: 目が笑っていなかった。
contrast_examples.en: Her eyes weren't smiling. (plain observation)

prompt.context_jp: うどん屋の前に着くと、美香はもう暖簾を出していた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 三年前から、この作業＿彼女ひとりの仕事になっている。
prompt.prompt_en: The line states a standing fact about 'this task.' Which particle fits?

feedback.correct_en: この作業 is the topic being characterized — 'as for this task, it has been hers alone for three years.' は sets it up as the theme the sentence then describes.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would push 'this task' as new, singled-out information answering 'which thing became her job,' but the sentence is a calm general statement about an ongoing arrangement, not an identification.

contrast_examples.jp: この作業は彼女の仕事だ。
contrast_examples.en: This task is her job. (describing the task)
THIS task is the problem. (singling it out)

prompt.context_jp: 厨房から出汁の湯気が立ち上り、
prompt.prompt_jp: 美香の額に汗＿浮かんでいた。
prompt.prompt_en: The narration notices sweat appearing on Mika's forehead. Which particle fits?

feedback.correct_en: This is a description of something coming into view — sweat appearing — so が marks 汗 as newly observed information, matching the parallel 湯気が立ち上り just before it.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would topicalize 'sweat' as if contrasting it with something else, which is out of place in a simple sensory observation of the scene.

contrast_examples.jp: 額に汗が浮かんでいた。
contrast_examples.en: Sweat had formed on her forehead. (noticing it)
The sweat had already dried. (as for the sweat)

prompt.context_jp: 「ときどきね」と大地は答えた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 気になる、と朱美は言わなかったが、その横顔＿そう言っていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Akemi didn't say it aloud, but something else 'said' it. Which particle fits the blank?

feedback.correct_en: が identifies the actual thing that conveyed the message: not her words but her profile. It answers 'what was it that said so?' against 朱美は言わなかった, so the contrast lands on 横顔.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would make 横顔 the topic and lose the pointed 'her words didn't, but her FACE did' identification the が delivers here.

contrast_examples.jp: 口では言わないが、目が語っていた。
contrast_examples.en: She didn't say it, but her eyes spoke. (identifying what spoke)

contrast_examples.jp: その横顔は寂しそうだった。
contrast_examples.en: Her profile looked lonely. (describing the profile)

prompt.context_jp: 駅を出ると、見覚えのある商店街の匂いが鼻に届いた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 蒼太＿改札を抜けるが早いか、駆け出して先に行ってしまった。
prompt.prompt_en: Souta's sudden dash is narrated as a fresh event. Which particle marks him in the blank?

feedback.correct_en: In a subordinate clause describing a sudden action (〜が早いか, 'no sooner than'), the actor takes が. Souta is the subject of the abrupt event, so 蒼太が is natural.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would lift Souta out as the sentence topic, which clashes with the tight, momentary 'the instant he passed the gate' framing that wants a plain が subject.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼が出るが早いか、雨が降り出した。
contrast_examples.en: No sooner had he left than it began to rain. (が in the time clause)
Souta is an energetic kid. (topic comment)

prompt.prompt_jp: 土曜日の朝、大宮行きの電車に揺られながら、大地は窓の外を流れる景色＿ぼんやりと眺めていた。
prompt.prompt_en: What was Daichi gazing at? Mark the object of 眺める.

feedback.correct_en: 眺める ('to gaze at') takes its object with を, so 景色を眺めていた is 'was gazing at the scenery.'
feedback.incorrect_en: が would make 景色 the subject (the scenery doing something), and に doesn't mark the thing looked at with this verb; both break the 'gaze at X' relationship.

contrast_examples.en: to gaze at the scenery (object)
the scenery spreads out (subject)

prompt.prompt_jp: 駅を出ると、見覚えのある商店街の匂いが鼻＿届いた。
prompt.prompt_en: The smell reached his nose. Which particle marks the destination?

feedback.correct_en: 届く ('to reach/arrive at') marks the goal with に, so 鼻に届いた means the scent reached as far as his nose.
feedback.incorrect_en: を would treat 鼻 as a direct object (the smell doesn't 'do' the nose), and で would mark a location of activity, neither of which expresses 'reached as far as.'

contrast_examples.en: The letter reached the house. (に goal)
I write a letter at home. (で location)

prompt.context_jp: 「おう、大ちゃん、また顔出してくれたか」
prompt.prompt_jp: と坂本さんは大地の肩＿叩いた。
prompt.prompt_en: Sakamoto-san patted Daichi's shoulder. Mark the thing being patted.

feedback.correct_en: 叩く ('to pat/strike') takes its target with を, so 肩を叩いた is 'patted (his) shoulder.'
feedback.incorrect_en: に would suggest patting toward the shoulder as a goal, which sounds unnatural with 叩く, and が would wrongly make the shoulder the subject.

contrast_examples.en: to pat the shoulder (object)
to knock on the door (object)

prompt.prompt_jp: とだけ答え、湯のみを両手＿包んだ。
prompt.prompt_en: He cupped the teacup using both hands. Which particle marks the means?

feedback.correct_en: で marks the instrument or means of an action — he wrapped the cup with/using both hands, so 両手で包んだ.
feedback.incorrect_en: に would mark a destination ('into both hands'), and を would make 両手 the object being wrapped, but here the hands are the means of wrapping the cup (湯のみを).

contrast_examples.en: to hold with both hands (で, means)
to eat with chopsticks (で, means)

prompt.context_jp: 「走らないで」と朱美が声を張ったが、
prompt.prompt_jp: その声には疲れが＿いた。
prompt.prompt_en: Fatigue was faintly seeping through her voice. Choose the verb that collocates with 疲れ here.

feedback.correct_en: 疲れがにじむ describes weariness 'seeping/showing through' subtly — exactly the quiet, faint tiredness in Akemi's voice.
feedback.incorrect_en: あふれる ('overflow') and こぼれる ('spill over') both imply a large, visible outpouring, too strong for the understated hint of fatigue the scene conveys.

contrast_examples.en: Fatigue shows faintly in the voice.
Smiles overflow. (abundant, visible)

prompt.prompt_jp: 坂本さんが暖簾を＿のは十一時過ぎだった。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the verb that idiomatically goes with 暖簾 (entering a shop by passing under the noren).

feedback.correct_en: 暖簾をくぐる ('to duck under the noren') is the set expression for stepping into a Japanese shop, since you pass beneath the hanging curtain.
feedback.incorrect_en: 暖簾を開ける treats the curtain like a door (you don't open a noren), and 渡る ('cross') doesn't fit entering through it — both miss the fixed idiom.

contrast_examples.en: to step in under the shop's noren
to open the door

prompt.prompt_jp: 大したことじゃないけど、と父は＿のように言っていた人だった。
prompt.prompt_en: His father said this phrase habitually. Choose the word that means a 'pet phrase / verbal habit.'

feedback.correct_en: 口癖 is a phrase someone says habitually; 口癖のように言う means he said it again and again as a matter of habit.
feedback.incorrect_en: 冗談 ('joke') and 自慢 ('boast') describe the content/tone, not the habitual repetition the sentence is pointing to with のように言っていた.

contrast_examples.jp: それが父の口癖だった。
contrast_examples.en: That was my father's pet phrase.
to tell a joke

prompt.prompt_jp: 話し合いの前に認識を揃えておきたい、と美香は＿口調を作って言ったが、その指先がわずかに震えているのが大地には見えた。
prompt.prompt_en: Mika deliberately put on a certain tone to mask her nerves. Which word describes that tone?

feedback.correct_en: 事務的な口調 ('businesslike tone') fits a deliberately neutral, matter-of-fact voice she 'constructs' (作って) to hold her composure — contrasted with her trembling fingertips.
feedback.incorrect_en: 感情的な ('emotional') is the opposite of the composure she's faking, and 親しげな ('friendly') doesn't match the careful, distancing way she frames a hard family discussion.

contrast_examples.en: to speak in a businesslike tone
to get emotional

prompt.prompt_jp: 彼女の足音が＿ように厨房と席の間を行き来した。
prompt.prompt_en: Her footsteps moved in a lively, springy way. Choose the verb that collocates with 足音 here.

feedback.correct_en: 足音が弾む conveys light, bouncing, energetic steps — capturing how briskly Mika hustles between kitchen and tables with each order.
feedback.incorrect_en: 響く ('resound') describes sound carrying, not liveliness, and 転がる ('roll') doesn't pair with footsteps in this sense; neither gives the springy energy 弾む does.

contrast_examples.en: to have a spring in one's step
footsteps echo (sound carrying)

prompt.prompt_jp: 彼女はガラス越しに＿をして、いつものように静かに去っていった。
prompt.prompt_en: Through the glass she gave a small, silent bow of acknowledgment. Choose the best word.

feedback.correct_en: 会釈 is a slight, courteous nod/bow — exactly the quiet greeting Tachibana-san gives through the glass before leaving.
feedback.incorrect_en: 握手 ('handshake') is impossible through glass, and 合図 ('a signal') implies communicating a message rather than the polite, restrained acknowledgment 会釈 describes.

contrast_examples.en: to give a slight bow/nod
to send a signal

prompt.context_jp: 坂本さんが暖簾をくぐったのは十一時過ぎだった。
prompt.prompt_en: Sakamoto-san is a longtime neighbor greeting Daichi warmly. Which line sounds more natural for him?

choices.text: 「おう、大ちゃん、また顔出してくれたか」
「こんにちは、大地様、またご来訪くださいましたか」

feedback.correct_en: A matches a familiar old neighbor: おう, the nickname 大ちゃん, and 顔出してくれたか are warm, casual, and natural for someone who's known Daichi for decades.
feedback.incorrect_en: B uses 様 and ご来訪くださいました — stiff business keigo that sounds absurdly formal between an old family friend and the son he watched grow up.

contrast_examples.jp: また顔出してくれたか。
contrast_examples.en: You came by again, huh. (warm/casual)

contrast_examples.jp: ご来訪くださいましたか。
contrast_examples.en: Have you graced us with a visit? (over-formal)

prompt.context_jp: 厨房から出汁の湯気が立ち上り、美香の額に汗が浮かんでいた。
prompt.prompt_en: Which ordering of the same elements reads more naturally?

choices.text: 注文を受けるたびに、彼女の足音が弾むように厨房と席の間を行き来した。
彼女の足音が厨房と席の間を、注文を受けるたびに弾むように行き来した。

feedback.correct_en: A leads with the time/condition clause (注文を受けるたびに), then subject, then the manner adverbial right before the verb — the smooth default Japanese flow.
feedback.incorrect_en: B jams the time clause in the middle and splits 厨房と席の間を from its verb, leaving the manner phrase stranded and the sentence choppy.

contrast_examples.jp: ベルが鳴るたびに、彼は急いで席を立った。
contrast_examples.en: Each time the bell rang, he hurriedly rose. (time clause first)

contrast_examples.jp: 彼は席を、ベルが鳴るたびに急いで立った。
contrast_examples.en: (awkwardly reordered)

prompt.context_jp: 「走らないで」と朱美が声を張ったが、
prompt.prompt_en: Which phrasing for 'fatigue showing in her voice' sounds natural?

choices.text: その声には疲れがにじんでいた。
その声には疲れが入っていた。

feedback.correct_en: 疲れがにじむ is the idiomatic way to say weariness 'shows/seeps through' a voice — natural and evocative.
feedback.incorrect_en: 疲れが入る ('fatigue enters') treats tiredness like a physical object placed inside the voice; it isn't a real collocation and sounds off.

contrast_examples.en: Weariness seeps into the voice. (natural)
(not idiomatic)

prompt.prompt_en: Which particle assignment reads naturally for 'the inside of the shop hadn't changed since father was alive'?

choices.text: 店の中は、父が生きていた頃と何ひとつ変わっていなかった。
店の中が、父は生きていた頃と何ひとつ変わっていなかった。

feedback.correct_en: A sets 店の中 as the topic (は) the sentence describes, and uses が inside the relative clause 父が生きていた頃 to mark 'father' as its subject — the natural division of labor.
feedback.incorrect_en: B reverses them: 店の中が forces an out-of-place 'it was THE SHOP that...' focus, and 父は inside the time clause stops it from cleanly modifying 頃, making the whole line awkward.

contrast_examples.jp: 部屋は、母が出かけた後も静かだった。
contrast_examples.en: The room stayed quiet after Mom left. (は topic / が in clause)

contrast_examples.jp: 部屋が、母は出かけた後も静かだった。
contrast_examples.en: (unnatural particle split)

prompt.prompt_en: The narration says Mika deliberately adopted a 事務的な口調 (businesslike tone) to open the discussion. Which line matches that chosen register?

choices.text: 「話し合いの前に認識を揃えておきたい」
「話す前に、ちゃんと分かり合っときたいんだけどさ」

feedback.correct_en: A's 認識を揃えておきたい is crisp, neutral, almost meeting-room phrasing — the deliberately businesslike distance Mika constructs to steady herself for a hard family talk.
feedback.incorrect_en: B (分かり合っときたいんだけどさ) is loose, casual sibling-speak; it would undercut the controlled, formal tone the narration says she's deliberately putting on.

contrast_examples.jp: 認識を揃えておきたい。
contrast_examples.en: I'd like to align our understanding. (businesslike)

contrast_examples.jp: 分かり合っときたいんだけどさ。
contrast_examples.en: I kinda wanna get on the same page, y'know. (casual)

prompt.context_jp: 美香はやかんを火にかけ、大地の前にお茶を置いた。
prompt.prompt_en: Mika is speaking to her older brother Daichi at home. Which line fits the register between siblings?

choices.text: 「お兄様、少々よろしいでしょうか」

feedback.correct_en: A's お兄ちゃん + ちょっといい is the warm, plain register a younger sister uses with her brother at the family shop.
feedback.incorrect_en: B's お兄様 and 少々よろしいでしょうか is formal keigo you'd use with a customer or superior — bizarrely distant for asking your own brother for a moment.

contrast_examples.jp: お兄ちゃん、ちょっといい？
contrast_examples.en: Hey, can I talk for a sec? (sibling-casual)

contrast_examples.jp: 少々よろしいでしょうか。
contrast_examples.en: Might I have a moment? (formal/customer)
